explanation:
## What actually happens

`v.erase(v.begin() + i)` removes the element at `i` and shifts
everything after it down one place. The element that was at `i+1` is now
at `i` — and the loop then does `++i` and skips straight past it.

The sample, step by step, with `lo = 0`, `hi = 10`:

| `i` | `v` before | `v[i]` | action | `v` after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `5 -1 -2 7 20 3` | 5 | keep | — |
| 1 | `5 -1 -2 7 20 3` | −1 | **erase** | `5 -2 7 20 3` |
| 2 | `5 -2 7 20 3` | 7 | keep | — |
| 3 | `5 -2 7 20 3` | 20 | **erase** | `5 -2 7 3` |
| 4 | `5 -2 7 3` | — | `i` is past the end; stop | — |

Output: two removed, `5 -2 7 3` kept. The `-2` was never examined,
because it slid into the slot the loop had just finished with.

## Why it passes review

With no two bad elements adjacent, every skipped element happens to be a
good one and the answer comes out right. The visible case
`1 2 3 4 5` removes nothing and is correct; `-1 -2 -3 -4` removes
alternate elements and is spectacularly wrong.

A bug that is correct on the easy inputs and wrong on the hard ones is
the worst kind to have, and "two of the bad things are next to each
other" is the kind of condition that does not occur in the test data
somebody wrote by hand.

## Three fixes

**Do not advance after an erase.** The smallest change:

```cpp
std::size_t i = 0;
while (i < v.size()) {
    if (bad(v[i])) { v.erase(v.begin() + i); ++removed; }
    else           { ++i; }
}
```

**Walk backwards.**

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = v.size(); i-- > 0; ) {
    if (bad(v[i])) { v.erase(v.begin() + i); ++removed; }
}
```

Erasing at `i` only moves elements after `i`, which the backward loop
has already dealt with. Note the `i-- > 0` idiom: counting down with an
unsigned index and `i >= 0` is an infinite loop, because an unsigned
value is never negative.

**Erase–remove.** The idiomatic one, and the only one that is not
quadratic:

```cpp
const auto it = std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), bad);
removed = static_cast<int>(v.end() - it);
v.erase(it, v.end());
```

`std::remove_if` does not remove anything. It moves the elements being
kept to the front, in order, and returns an iterator to just past the
last of them; the actual shortening is the `erase`. In C++20 the free
function `std::erase_if(v, bad)` does both and returns the count.

## The cost

The first two fixes are `O(n^2)`: each erase shifts the tail. With 50,000
readings and most of them bad that is over a billion moves. Erase–remove
is one pass and one shift, so `O(n)`.

For this exercise any of the three passes. In anything that runs on real
data, the third is the one to reach for — and the reason it exists at
all is that removing from the middle of a contiguous container is
expensive however carefully you write the loop.
